readout_other: Extracellular action-potential (spike) recordings in S1BF; head-turning behavioural test
direction_notes: Ultrasound delivered via the head-mounted stimulator increased extracellular spike firing in S1BF during stimulation and evoked head-turning responses toward the stimulated hemisphere significantly more often than sham (no coupling gel) stimulation.
safety_notes: Mice were observed for over 1 month after stimulation experiments with no abnormal behaviour.

exposures.label: Head-mounted ultrasound stimulation of primary somatosensory cortex barrel field (S1BF) in freely moving mice

timing.protocol_description: A series of 2-MHz ultrasound stimuli was delivered to each mouse in a 360-s trial for electrophysiology (stimulus repetition period 6 s). For head-turning tests, two head-mounted stimulators (left and right S1BF) delivered the same stimulus parameters alternately every 6 s; control trials used the same procedure but without acoustic coupling gel so no ultrasound entered the brain.

source_quotes.n_subjects: 17 male C57BL/6 mice that were 10–12 weeks old and weighed 23 g ( 15%) were randomly divided into two groups: (1) ultrasound stimuli and spike acquisition (group US-SPIKE, $n = 4 )$ , (2) ultrasound stimuli and head-turning (group US-HEAD, $n = 1 3 )$ .
source_quotes.exposures[0].fundamental_frequency_khz: Considering the size of the mouse brain and the ultrasound attenuation of the mouse skull, a piece of disk-shaped piezoelectric ceramic (5 mm in diameter and 1 mm thick) with a resonant frequency of 2 MHz was adapted for the ultrasound stimulator.

flags.reason: PRF converted from the stated pulse repetition period T2 = 1 ms via the paper's own formula PRF = 1/T2, not independent arithmetic.
US-SPIKE mice received one 360-s recording trial; US-HEAD mice received many alternating stimuli within a single behavioural test session; paper does not define a discrete session count.

Values (P0, Isppa, Ispta) given in the Stimulus Parameters/Results section are transducer output values in the acoustic focal region; not explicitly stated as pre- versus post-skull, though a separate ~3 dB skull attenuation is reported elsewhere without being applied to this specific stimulus.
